summary: A little-known insect-eating slit-faced bat of semi-arid and moist woodland savannah, including mopane woodland in the far north of Kruger. It roosts in hollow baobabs and sausage trees, sandstone caves, rock fissures, mine adits and buildings, forages in clutter on moths, beetles and flies, and is listed as Near Threatened in the 2025 regional assessment and as Least Concern on the global IUCN Red List (2017).
description: A slit-faced bat of the family Nycteridae. The 2025 EWT assessment, citing Monadjem et al. (2020), describes short, broad wings that allow manoeuvrable flight, and gives mean forearm lengths of about 4.1 cm in females and 3.9 cm in males, with mean total lengths of about 10.2 cm and 9.6 cm respectively. The same assessment, and the 2016 assessment before it, call it a whispering echolocating bat that is difficult to monitor acoustically and that avoids mist nets. Pelage colour, the form of the facial slit, ear shape and other coat marks were not described in the sources used, so those details are not filled in here. The English name in species-list.json is Wood's slit-faced bat, which matches the lead English name on the 2025 and 2016 EWT assessments; those assessments also list Wood's Long-eared Bat. The species-list form is kept.
habits: The 2025 EWT assessment, following Cotterill (2013) and earlier sources, says the natural history of this species is not well known. It roosts by day in hollow trees, particularly baobabs (Adansonia digitata) and sausage trees (Kigelia africana), and also in sandstone caves, rock fissures, mine adits and buildings (Ansell 1967; Cotterill 1996, 2013; Skinner and Chimimba 2005). In the assessment region it is recorded from the Mopane Bioregion. Colonies are reported as a few dozen up to 40-50 individuals (Cotterill 2013; Monadjem et al. 2020), or as mixed-sex colonies of up to 50 (Cotterill 2013); animals have also been recorded singly (ACR 2015). It is a clutter forager with short, broad wings and low wing-loading (Monadjem et al. 2010, 2020). Movement patterns are listed as unknown, but the 2025 assessment says that, owing to low wing-loading, the species is unlikely to be capable of long-distance movement or migration, and it refers to a resident population that appears continuous with the Zimbabwean population through the Great Limpopo Transfrontier Park and the Greater Mapungubwe Transfrontier Conservation Area. The assessment names Kruger National Park among the four collection areas in the region, and records one Pafuri (KNP) observation in July 2006 (C. Schoeman unpubl. data), while also stating that further field studies are needed to confirm continued presence in the assessment region.

diet.summary: An insectivore and clutter forager. The 2025 and 2016 EWT assessments, citing Monadjem et al. (2010), say it feeds mainly on Lepidoptera, Coleoptera and Diptera.

young: Limited reproductive data. The 2025 EWT assessment, citing Monadjem et al. (2020), says the species seems to be a summer breeder, and, citing Cotterill (2013), that it is suspected to show seasonal monoestry, with pregnant females recorded in mid-August and November, and one pup per litter. Gestation time, size at birth, age at maturity and generation length are listed as unknown on that page. No Kruger-specific breeding study was found in the sources used.

prey.note: A main prey group in the 2025 and 2016 EWT assessments (Monadjem et al. 2010). Not mammals in this guide.

habitat: The 2025 EWT assessment, citing Cotterill (2013), places the species in semi-arid and moist woodland savannahs, including miombo and mopane woodlands, where suitable day roosts are available. In the assessment region it is recorded from the Mopane Bioregion of extreme northern Limpopo, including Kruger National Park. Day roosts are hollow trees, especially baobabs and sausage trees, and also sandstone caves, rock fissures, mine adits and buildings. The 2016 assessment, citing Meester et al. (1986), says it is typically restricted to below 1,000 m above sea level, although the Zambian type specimen was collected at 1,250 m. The 2025 assessment gives a wider elevation range of 49-1,417 m (Monadjem et al. 2024). Both figures are recorded; a more detailed Kruger-specific habitat account was not given beyond the Pafuri record and the statement that the species has been recorded in the park.

population.notes: No Kruger census or SANParks park-wide count was found. The 2025 regional assessment describes abundance as not well known, lists the species as one of the rarest African nycterids, gives a regional population trend of declining in the page header and suspected to be declining in the population account, and gives the number of mature individuals in the largest subpopulation as possibly 250, based on Cotterill (2013). Those figures are not a park-wide Kruger count. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf

research.note: This file follows species-list.json in treating the Kruger animal as Nycteris woodi (English Wood's slit-faced bat; Afrikaans Wood se spleetneusvlermuis) and does not remap the names. The 2025 EWT /project/ page was found from the Chiroptera tag page, not by guessing the slug, and its body does describe this species. Status is set to resident because that page gives a definite Kruger record (including Pafuri, July 2006) and does not describe a migrant or seasonal movement pattern; it lists movement as unknown but unlikely to include long-distance movement or migration, and refers to a resident population. The same page asks for surveys to confirm continued presence in the assessment region, which is flagged in gaps. Regional status is Near Threatened (2025, no change from 2016); the global IUCN listing is Least Concern (2017). No licensed photographs were found in iNaturalist place 69020 or place 6986. iNaturalist place 69020 returned 0 sound observations for taxon 41190. Pelage and facial marks were not described in the sources used and were not copied from Nycteris thebaica. A later pass searched iNaturalist place 113055 and Wikimedia Commons (Nycteris woodi and the synonym Nycteris sabiensis); the only licensed southern African photographs were of handled, in-hand or grounded bats, and Commons had only museum skins and skulls, so images remain empty.

gaps: No Kruger census or SANParks population figure was found. The 2025 regional assessment gives a suspected declining regional trend and a largest-subpopulation figure of possibly 250 mature individuals (Cotterill 2013), which is not a park-wide count. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf

The 2025 EWT assessment records the species from Kruger National Park, including a Pafuri record in July 2006, but also says further field studies are needed to confirm its continued presence in the assessment region. Status is still set to resident, because the Kruger record is definite and the page does not describe a migrant or seasonal movement pattern.

The Afrikaans name in species-list.json is Wood se spleetneusvlermuis. The 2025 and 2016 EWT assessments list Wood se Speetneusvlermuis, Wood-spleetneusvlermuis (Wood-Spleetneusvlermuis in the 2025 page) and Woodse Langoorvlermuis. The species-list form is kept.
The English name in species-list.json is Wood's slit-faced bat, which matches the lead EWT English name. The 2025 and 2016 assessments also list Wood's Long-eared Bat. The species-list form is kept.

Historically two subspecies were recognised (N. w. sabensis / sabiensis and N. w. woodi); the 2025 and 2016 assessments no longer distinguish them, and they do not include N. parisii. The 2016 synonym line uses Nycteris sabiensis Roberts 1946, while the taxonomic note uses sabensis; the 2025 synonym line uses Nycteris woodi Roberts, 1946 ssp. sabiensis. The file keeps the species-list.json names and does not assign Kruger animals to a subspecies.

Pelage colour, facial-slit form, ear shape, iris colour and other coat marks were not described in the sources used. Those marks are left null and were not copied from Nycteris thebaica. No sourced field comparison with N. thebaica was found, so a similar-species entry was omitted.

Mass, shoulder height, head-and-body length and tail length were not published in the sources used. The 2025 page gives sex-specific mean forearm and total lengths, and maximum forearm lengths, after Monadjem et al. (2020); the total-length figures were not entered as head-and-body length.

Elevation figures disagree: the 2016 assessment, citing Meester et al. (1986), says the species is typically restricted to below 1,000 m (type specimen 1,250 m); the 2025 assessment gives 49-1,417 m (Monadjem et al. 2024). Both are quoted in the habitat text.

Colony-size figures differ slightly between sources used on the 2025 page: up to 40-50 individuals (Cotterill 2013; Monadjem et al. 2020) and mixed-sex colonies of up to 50 (Cotterill 2013). The 2016 assessment gave up to 40 (Monadjem et al. 2010). All are quoted.
The 2025 assessment states there are no predation records. No predator list was entered.

iNaturalist place 69020 (Kruger) returned 0 licensed photographs and 0 sound observations for taxon 41190. A follow-up licensed-photo query for place 6986 also returned 0. The images array is empty. The calls account is limited to the whispering-echolocation wording in the EWT assessments; no licensable recording was found.
Animal Diversity Web has only a classification stub for this taxon. Wikipedia is a short stub and was used only for the 2017 IUCN citation.
No Kruger-specific breeding study was found. Gestation is listed as unknown on the 2025 page.

A later search of iNaturalist place 113055 found only handled, in-hand or grounded photographs (Great Dyke, Guruve, Zimbabwe; Chilo Gorge, Zimbabwe). Wikimedia Commons under Nycteris woodi has only museum skins and skulls, and Nycteris sabiensis returned none. The images array remains empty.
